newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Lonrho profit falls, cautious on JCI talks.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lonrho profit falls, cautious on JCI talks.

text.p: British conglomerate Lonrho Plc, which is in the throes of a major shake-up, on Monday reported lower first-half profits, while making clear the end of its planned overhaul is not in sight yet.
Lonrho's talks to merge the mining business with South Africa's JCI Ltd continue, but the British group emphasised the negotiations, first announced last month, were still in a preliminary stage.
"It is too early to say whether a merger is possible or likely. Talks are continuing, but there is no commitment," chief executive Nick Morrell told Reuters.
A Lonrho-JCI merger would create a global mining powerhouse with a market capitalisation of than three billion dollars.
Morrell, meanwhile, expected the long awaited sale of Lonrho's Princess hotels to be completed by end-September after negotiations began last year.
The planned demerger of the African trading business was complex, but Lonrho expects it to be "well advanced" by the end of this year.
The ongoing merger, split-up and divestment talks are part of Lonrho's strategy, devised in 1995 and frequently adjusted afterwards, to streamline its operations.
Lonrho's first-half pre-tax profit fell to 38 million pounds ($62.9 million) from 61 million, coming in exactly as analysts had expected.
The results exclude a net profit on disposal earlier this year of Lonrho Sugar for 129 million pounds. This was used to repay all central debts, Lonrho said.
Pre-tax results were hit by depressed precious metal prices in the six months to March 31, the strength of the pound and subdued trading in the African business, Lonrho said.
A lower contribution of Ghana's Ashanti Goldfields Co Ltd, in which Lonrho has a 41 percent interest, also depressed profits.
South African mining giant Anglo American Corp of South Africa and, most recently, it rival Gencor Ltd are said to be interested in acquiring the Ashanti stake.
But Lonrho wants to stick to its holding. "Ashanti is a very important asset and we have no plans at this stage to divest it," Morrell said.
Industry analysts had feared Ashanti might be passed on to Anglo under some sort of "sweetheart" agreement to soften the pain for Anglo in giving up its Lonrho stake.
Anglo built up its 28 percent holding last year, but was forced by the European Union in April to reduce its stake to below 10 percent.
The EU believed Anglo's 28 percent interest would give it control over Lonrho and subsequent dominance in the world platinum market. ($ = 0.604 British Pounds)
